58:10.text: And it came to pass in those days, that he went out into a mountain to pray, and continued all night in prayer to God.

provenance.other: 'In prayer to God' occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Luke 6:12. The other half of the clause is the pour-out-the-soul idiom, which the KJV has twice and in two grammatical forms: Psalm 42:4's present 'I pour out my soul in me' and 1 Samuel 1:15's past 'I have poured out my soul before the LORD'. Alma 58:10 has the present, which is the Psalm's; 'pour out our' occurs in no KJV verse at all.
provenance.alternative: That the four words are an unremarkable English construction anyone could compose independently. The count says otherwise about the KJV, but not about 1829.
provenance.significance: Recover Luke 6:12 and the phrase turns out to belong, in the King James Bible, to one man on one night: it is the vigil Jesus keeps alone on a mountain, and it is the only all-night prayer the Gospels give him. What Alma 58 does with it is hand it to an army. A body of starving soldiers in a fortified camp prays in the words the KJV reserves for Christ's solitary vigil, and the next verse answers them the way Luke's vigil is answered — with a naming and a sending. Luke's morning produces the twelve; Helaman's produces the assurance, the peace, and the two thousand who do not die.

58:10.note: 'Therefore we did pour out our souls in prayer to God, that he would strengthen us and deliver us out of the hands of our enemies.' Two KJV idioms meet in one clause and neither is the war-narrative language the chapter has been running for nine verses. The pouring out of the soul is the Psalter's and Hannah's — private, distressed, and answered; 'in prayer to God' is a Lukan singleton. Held at moderate because the second is only four words long and the shared vocabulary with the first is two; what argues for the row is that a chapter otherwise built out of provisions, spies and strong holds changes register entirely for one sentence, and changes into scripture's register.

58:11.text: I will hear what God the LORD will speak: for he will speak peace unto his people, and to his saints: but let them not turn again to folly.

provenance.other: 'Speak peace' occurs in exactly three KJV verses: Psalm 28:3, Psalm 85:8 and Zechariah 9:10. Only one of the three has God as the speaker and a people as the hearer, and that is Psalm 85:8. The preposition is the awkward datum — 'speak peace to' with 'to' rather than 'unto' is itself a KJV singleton, and it belongs to Psalm 28:3, where the workers of iniquity 'speak peace to their neighbours, but mischief is in their hearts'. Alma 58:11 has Psalm 28's preposition and Psalm 85's sense.
provenance.significance: Psalm 85 is not a psalm of private consolation; it is a national one, addressed to a land God has already once turned back from captivity and asking him to do it again — 'Wilt thou not revive us again: that thy people may rejoice in thee?' The verse the Book of Mormon borrows is the psalm's hinge, the moment the speaker stops petitioning and listens for the answer, and what follows it is 'Surely his salvation is nigh them that fear him; that glory may dwell in our land'. Helaman's epistle is a report on whether glory will dwell in the land, written by a man who has just told the chief judge he fears the judgments of God on it. The psalm supplies not only the phrase but the shape of the paragraph: petition (58:10), a pause to hear (58:11), and an answer about the land.

58:11.note: 'Insomuch that he did speak peace to our souls, and did grant unto us as great faith, and did cause us that we should hope for our deliverance in him.' The answer to the prayer of 58:10 is given in the words of the one KJV verse in which God speaks peace to a people, and the sentence keeps the psalm's sequence — the speaking, then the hope. Held at moderate because the object is changed from 'his people' to 'our souls', which is the Book of Mormon's own idiom rather than the psalm's; the 1830's 'as great faith', flattened to 'great faith' in 1920, preserves a comparative whose second term the sentence never supplies.

58:40.text: Stand fast therefore in the liberty wherewith Christ hath made us free, and be not entangled again with the yoke of bondage.

provenance.other: 'Liberty wherewith' is a KJV singleton, and so is the whole run 'wherewith Christ hath made us free'. 'Stand fast' occurs in nine KJV verses and is Pauline in seven of them; the Book of Mormon has taken the one where it governs liberty. 'Made them free' occurs in no KJV verse, which is the mark of the substitution: the phrase had to be re-pronouned to fit.
provenance.significance: The book of Alma has been quarrying Galatians 5:1 for fifteen chapters, and always from the back end. Moroni throws the yoke of bondage at Zerahemnah (44:2); the narrator uses it twice of Amalickiah (49:7, 49:26); the whole political vocabulary of the war chapters — liberty, freedom, bondage — is the vocabulary of that one verse. What happens at 58:40 is that the front half finally arrives, and it arrives attached to the two thousand young men. The verse's substitution is the argument: Paul writes 'the liberty wherewith Christ hath made us free' of a freedom from the law, and Helaman writes 'that liberty wherewith God hath made them free' of soldiers who have received many wounds and lost no one. Read Galatians back into it and the sentence claims that the political liberty these chapters have spent twenty pages defending with swords is the same liberty Paul tells the Galatians not to trade for a yoke — and the clause is picked up and repeated word for word three chapters later, when Pahoran closes his reply to Moroni by blessing 'all those who stand fast in that liberty wherewith God hath made them free' (61:21). Whatever else divides the two epistles, they end in the same borrowed sentence.

58:40.note: 'Nevertheless they stand fast in that liberty wherewith God hath made them free.' The clause reproduces Galatians 5:1's opening entire, with two changes and no others: 'therefore in the' becomes 'in that', and 'Christ hath made us free' becomes 'God hath made them free'. 'Liberty wherewith' occurs in exactly one KJV verse. This falls well below Skousen's sixteen-word threshold and is not one of his thirty-six, but it is a complete clause taken from a verse the chapter can be shown to know at both ends — 58:41 immediately returns to it, 'the Lord our God who hath redeemed us and made us free' — and the argument for its earlier half was made at Alma 44:2. The 1830's 'hath' was modernized to 'has' in 1920, so the first edition preserves the KJV's verb form as well as its words.
